Me. Whoever comes, whoever goes, I open up. Trevor at half seven, Ms Quinn at quarter past eight. There’s a camera in the lobby; the boss had it put in. And… yesterday the boss told me, ‘Sid, tomorrow morning take me to Pilsen, to bube.’ Don’t tell the lawyers, he said.
He adjusts the wire in his ear.
Who was at the door in the evening?

· Trevor Kincaid on a monthly allowance this past year; no debts, his share of the estate tied to a foundation.
· 43 payments over the last two years from Lakeshore Freight to a port shipping company in Napoli; ‘E. V.’ in the approval box of each.
· All the payments were processed by: the finance directorate.

· Severe hypoglycaemia; blood sugar too low to measure.
· Insulin level in the blood about five times the normal evening dose.
· A single needle mark on the abdomen. Time of death: 22.30–00.30.
· Only water in the glass on the desk.

· The cartridge in the pen: five-times-concentrated (U-500) insulin; the pen is set for a standard (U-100) cartridge. U-500 is not on the victim’s prescription.
· Marjorie Quinn’s fingerprint on the cartridge’s glass.
· In the fridge, nothing is missing from the U-100 cartridges besides the one the housekeeper fitted; in the bin, a U-100 cartridge, full, unused.
· Pharmacy record: on 9 September a box of U-500, on a prescription in the name of Marjorie Quinn’s mother, was collected by Marjorie Quinn.
The cartridge in the pen was swapped for one five times stronger

He did his evening dose himself every night at 22.00; I prepared the pen on his desk. I keep the cartridges in the fridge and count every one. Last night I put the pen on the desk at 20.00; there was a new cartridge in it, I fitted it.
She straightens the collar of her tunic.
How did Mr Kincaid use his insulin?

Trevor at 19.30; they shouted, he walked out. Then Ms Quinn came; she was in the room with the gentleman from 20.30 to 21.30. The door was shut; at one point the gentleman asked for water and I brought it. Ms Quinn was standing at the desk, next to the pen.
Who went into the study in the evening?
Lakeshore Freight’s founder is dead in his Gold Coast flat. The day before, he had called bube.
The company’s financial information is confidential.
A fingerprint? I touched everything while I was showing him the accounts.

For twenty years I carried that company; not the trucks, the money. One morning Walter was going to go to bube and tell them everything — Paris, Tokyo, Napoli, her. That woman never forgives. I swapped the cartridge in the pen for one five times stronger. He did it with his own hand. And yes, that voice is mine. I told Edda Napoli was ready. You won’t find her; she’s already there.
You swapped the cartridge in the pen.
The quarterly accounts. Walter was tired, old; he’d been confused these last few days. I left at 21.40. I never touched his insulin — why would I?
She touches her diamond earring and lowers her hand.
Why were you there in the evening?
I took a lipstick out of my bag. Are you going to interpret that too?

On the morning of 13 September 2030, in a penthouse flat on the Gold Coast, Lakeshore Freight’s founder Walter Kincaid (74) was found dead at his desk. The victim had type 1 diabetes; his insulin pen was on the desk.

The housekeeper Lupe Ochoa found the body at 07.10. Present in the flat the previous evening: his son Trevor Kincaid, finance director Marjorie Quinn, driver Sid Abrams, housekeeper Lupe Ochoa.
Request the pen, cartridge and pharmacy analysis

The housekeeper gave the pen and the woman at the desk, the driver the victim’s last plan. The medical line gave the print on the cartridge and the pharmacy, the audio line the night’s conversations. The accounts line tied 43 payments to Napoli.
Every truck in Chicago was heading for the same port. Next city: Napoli.

After the arrests in Chicago, Lakeshore Freight’s founder Walter Kincaid decided to tell bube everything. The evening finance director Marjorie Quinn learned of it, she swapped the cartridge in the insulin pen the housekeeper had prepared for one five times stronger, and as she left the room she told someone, ‘Tell Edda, Napoli is ready.’ Kincaid took his evening dose with his own hand.

12 September:

· 20.36 Walter Kincaid: ‘Marjorie, tomorrow I’m going to Pilsen. I suggest you find yourself a lawyer.’
· 20.37 Marjorie Quinn: ‘Walter, that isn’t your decision.’
· 20.51 Marjorie Quinn (on the phone as she leaves the room, door ajar): ‘Tell Edda, Napoli is ready. The old man won’t see the morning.’
· 21.58 Walter Kincaid, alone: ‘Evening dose.’ The click of the pen.
I’ve nothing to do with my father’s company.

I asked for money, like always. He wouldn’t give it. ‘We’re going to lose everything tomorrow anyway, Trevor, and so am I,’ he said. I didn’t understand what he meant. I left at 19.50; I was at a bar in Wicker Park until morning.
He pushes up his shirt sleeves.
Why did you shout at your father?
